findings.title: Federated recovery codes are never consumed and can be replayed
findings.body: isValid for recovery-authn-codes accepts a submitted code if it equals any value in the stored JSON list and then returns true without removing that code. Combined with getCredentials, which rebuilds the credential via createFromValues from the original full list (all codes unused), a code that has already been used still validates on every later login. Recovery codes are single-use bearer credentials; this storage, which is the implementation the new test relies on, leaves them reusable indefinitely. The new test only logs in once with the first code, so it does not catch the replay.

findings.title: Successful federated recovery-code login does not retire the credential
findings.body: After credentialManager().isValid succeeds, the authenticator loads the credential and, when all codes are used, calls removeStoredCredentialById. That API only deletes a credential stored in Keycloak's local credential store. A recovery-code credential created through CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential lives in the user-storage provider when updateCredential returns true, and nothing in this path calls the storage's updateCredential or disableCredentialType to drop or rewrite the used code. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider used to mark the code used inside isValid; that provider is skipped once user storage owns the credential. Exhausted or already-used federated codes therefore stay valid, and the required-action fallback never sees allCodesUsed() if the storage returns a freshly rebuilt unused model.

findings.title: User storage is given every recovery code in plaintext
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes with JsonSerialization and passes that string as the UserCredentialModel challenge response. Local storage stores only hashes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues / hashRawCode). Any user-storage provider that persists challengeResponse, as the new backwards-compatibility storage does in credentialData, keeps the full set of unused backup codes in cleartext. A compromise of that store exposes codes that can be submitted directly to isValid.
